concepts.name: Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole
concepts.why: All magnets attract iron, but a magnet brought near another magnet may attract it or repel it, and experiment shows that this is because every magnet has two ends that behave differently. If a magnet is freely suspended, one end points toward the north, and the two ends are named the north magnetic pole and the south magnetic pole for the directions they seek. Naming the two ends is the first step in the subject, because every later rule of the chapter, from the direction of a field line to the torque on a loop, is stated in terms of them.
concepts.evidence: The section's first learning objective asks the reader to describe the difference between the north and south poles of a magnet, the suspended magnet of Figure 22.4 is the experiment that names them, and the glossary defines both terms.

concepts.name: Like poles repel and unlike poles attract
concepts.why: Bringing two magnets together shows that two north poles push each other apart, two south poles do the same, and a north pole and a south pole pull together. The rule is worth stating beside the electrostatic one, unlike charges attract and like charges repel, because the two look alike and the reader will be tempted to carry the whole of electrostatics across; the chapter's later sections show where the analogy holds and where it breaks.
concepts.evidence: The book prints the rule in its own boxed note, Universal Characteristics of Magnets and Magnetic Poles, Figure 22.5 draws both cases with force arrows, and the section's Take-Home Experiment asks the reader to show it with two refrigerator magnets.

concepts.name: North and south poles cannot be separated
concepts.why: Cut a bar magnet in half and you do not get a north pole in one hand and a south pole in the other; you get two shorter magnets, each with both poles. Cut again and the same thing happens, down to the iron atom itself. This is where the analogy with charge fails, since a positive charge and a negative charge separate easily, and it is the fact that later forces the chapter to explain all magnetism as current: a current loop always produces a pair of poles and never a single one.
concepts.evidence: Figure 22.6 splits a magnet again and again, the section summary states that it is not possible to isolate north and south poles, and 22.2 returns to the fact to argue that electric current is the source of all magnetism.

concepts.name: Ferromagnetic materials and magnetization
concepts.why: Only a few materials, iron, cobalt, nickel, gadolinium and some rare earth alloys among them, show strong magnetic effects. These are called ferromagnetic, after ferrum, the Latin word for iron. They do more than respond to a magnet: they can be magnetized themselves, which means they can be induced to be magnetic or made into permanent magnets, and this is why a magnet held near an unmagnetized piece of iron attracts it.
concepts.evidence: The section's first learning objective asks the reader to define ferromagnet, Figure 22.7 shows an unmagnetized bar being made into a permanent magnet between two others, and the glossary defines both ferromagnetic and magnetized.

concepts.name: Domains and how a material becomes magnetized
concepts.why: Inside a ferromagnetic material there are regions called domains, each of which acts like a small bar magnet because the poles of its individual atoms are aligned. In an unmagnetized object the domains are small and point in random directions, so their effects cancel. In an external magnetic field the domains that already point the right way grow at the expense of the others and the rest swing into line, and the material as a whole becomes a magnet. Heating it and cooling it, or tapping it while the field is applied, makes the alignment permanent.
concepts.evidence: The second learning objective asks the reader to describe the role of magnetic domains in magnetization, Figure 22.8 draws the same piece of iron with random domains, with partly aligned domains and as a single domain, and the AP items ask how the domains of an iron rod respond to an external field and how a rod is made permanently magnetic.

concepts.name: The Curie temperature
concepts.why: Thermal motion works against the alignment of domains, so heating a permanent magnet in the absence of another magnet demagnetizes it, as do hard blows. For each ferromagnetic material there is a well-defined temperature, the Curie temperature, above which it cannot be magnetized at all; for iron it is 1043 K, which is 770 °C and well above room temperature. Some elements and alloys have Curie temperatures below room temperature and are ferromagnetic only when they are cold.
concepts.evidence: The third learning objective asks the reader to explain the significance of the Curie temperature, the section states the value for iron, and the glossary defines the term.

concepts.name: Electromagnets: a current makes a magnet
concepts.why: Oersted found in 1820 that a compass needle is deflected by a current-carrying wire, the first evidence that moving charge has anything to do with magnets. Using an electric current to make a magnet is called electromagnetism, and a magnet made this way is an electromagnet. Iron filings scattered round a current-carrying coil arrange themselves in the same pattern they take round a bar magnet, and an electromagnet has north and south poles that cannot be separated and that repel and attract by the same rule, so the two kinds of magnet are the same kind of thing.
concepts.evidence: The fourth learning objective asks the reader to describe the relationship between electricity and magnetism, Figure 22.10 sets the filings round a coil beside the filings round a bar magnet, and Figures 22.9, 22.11 and 22.12 give the MRI magnet, the ferromagnetic core and the recording head as applications.

concepts.name: Electric current is the source of all magnetism
concepts.why: An electromagnet makes a field with a current, and the section argues that a ferromagnet does too, at a scale too small to see: an electron in orbit about a nucleus is a closed current loop, and the electron's spin is a second current, and both produce a magnetic field with a north pole and a south pole. Ferromagnetism is the cooperative alignment of these spins. The argument rests on the fact that isolated poles are never found, because a current loop always produces a pair of poles, and it is the sentence the rest of the chapter is built on.
concepts.evidence: The book prints the statement in a boxed note of its own, Electric Currents and Magnetism, Figure 22.13 draws the planetary orbit and the spinning electron as current loops, and the section discusses the continuing search for magnetic monopoles.

concepts.name: The magnetic field represents magnetic forces
concepts.why: A compass needle feels a force with nothing touching it, and to describe forces that act at a distance the book defines a field, as it did for gravity and for electric charge. The magnetic field is that representation for magnetic forces, and it is traditionally called the B-field. A field is a way of mapping the forces that surround an object and can act on another object at a distance, and it represents the object that generates it, not the probe that tests it.
concepts.evidence: The section's one learning objective asks the reader to define magnetic field, the book prints a boxed note, Making Connections: Concept of a Field, setting the gravitational, electric and magnetic fields side by side, and the glossary defines magnetic field and B-field.

concepts.name: Field lines point the way a compass points
concepts.why: The field is drawn with magnetic field lines, a pictorial tool for showing its strength and its direction. The direction of the lines is defined to be the direction in which the north end of a small compass needle points, which makes the definition something the reader can check with a compass on a table. Small compasses do not disturb the field they test, just as a small test charge does not disturb an electric field, so the map they trace is a map of the magnet alone.
concepts.evidence: Figure 22.14 sets compasses all round a bar magnet, joins their arrows into continuous lines and then shows the lines closing inside the magnet, and the glossary defines both magnetic field lines and the direction of magnetic field lines.

concepts.name: The four rules for magnetic field lines
concepts.why: Mapping many fields has settled four rules. The field is tangent to the field line at every point, so a compass lies along the line. The strength of the field is proportional to how closely the lines are packed, exactly to the number of lines crossing a unit area held perpendicular to them. Lines never cross, because the field has one value at each point in space. And the lines are continuous closed loops with no beginning and no end, which is the deepest of the four, since electric field lines begin and end on charges and magnetic lines have no monopoles to begin or end on.
concepts.evidence: The section prints the four rules as a numbered list and repeats them in its summary, its conceptual questions ask why crossing lines would make the field ambiguous and how magnetic and electric field lines differ, and Figure 22.15 draws the closed loops of a current loop and a straight wire with the dot and cross symbols for a field out of and into the page.

concepts.name: The magnetic force on a moving charge, $\kF = \kq\kv\kBmag\sin\theta$
concepts.why: A magnetic field exerts a force on a charge only while the charge moves, and the size of that force is the charge times the speed times the field strength times the sine of the angle between the velocity and the field. The sine matters as much as the rest: a charge moving along a field line feels no force at all, and a charge moving across the lines feels the most. This force is often called the Lorentz force, and it is the mechanism by which one magnet pushes another, since every magnet is made of moving charge.
concepts.evidence: The result is the section's first equation and its third learning objective, the section summary restates it, Example 22.1 computes the force on a charged glass rod thrown through the Earth's field, and eight of the section's problems ask for one of its four factors.

concepts.name: Field strength is defined by the force, $\kBmag = \kF/\kq\kv\sin\theta$
concepts.why: The book has not said until now what a magnetic field strength is, only what a field line looks like, and it settles the question by turning the force law round. Solving for $B$ defines the strength of a field as the force per unit charge per unit velocity, measured across the field, exactly as the electric field strength was defined as the force per unit charge. A definition of this kind is worth noticing, because it says the field is known only through what it does to a moving charge.
concepts.evidence: The section states that this is how the magnetic field strength is defined, prints the rearranged equation, and uses it at once to work out what the unit of field strength must be.

concepts.name: The tesla and the gauss
concepts.why: Because the sine is a pure number, the unit of magnetic field strength follows from the definition: one tesla is one newton per coulomb per metre per second, which is one newton per ampere-metre. A smaller unit, the gauss, is $10^{-4}$ tesla. The numbers are worth carrying: the strongest permanent magnets reach about 2 T, superconducting electromagnets 10 T or more, and the Earth's field at the surface only about $5 \times 10^{-5}$ T, which is half a gauss, and that last number explains why the reader never feels the Earth pushing on the charge in a pocket.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the unit from the definition, prints the identity, names the gauss in its glossary, and uses the Earth's value in Example 22.1 and in five of its problems.

concepts.name: Right hand rule 1 for the force on a moving charge
concepts.why: The direction of the magnetic force is perpendicular to the plane formed by the velocity and the field, which is not a direction that can be read off a flat drawing without a convention, so the book gives one. Point the thumb of the right hand along the velocity, the fingers along the field, and the force on a positive charge comes out of the palm. One velocity, one thumb; many field lines, many fingers; the force is the way you would push. The force on a negative charge is exactly opposite.
concepts.evidence: The second learning objective asks the reader to use the rule, Figure 22.16 draws the hand with the three vectors, Figure 22.17 applies it to a charged rod thrown west, and six of the section's problems ask for one of the three directions given the other two.

concepts.name: The force reverses when the sign of the charge reverses
concepts.why: Right hand rule 1 is stated for a positive charge, and the force on a negative charge moving the same way is in exactly the opposite direction. This is worth separating from the rule itself, because the charges that actually move in a wire are electrons and the reader will spend the rest of the chapter translating between the direction of a conventional current and the direction the carriers travel. It is also what makes the Hall effect able to say which sign of carrier is moving.
concepts.evidence: The section states the reversal immediately after the rule, the caption of Figure 22.17 notes that a negative charge in the same situation feels a force straight up, and two of the section's problems are the earlier ones repeated for a negative charge.

concepts.name: The magnetic force does no work on the charge
concepts.why: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, and a force perpendicular to the motion does no work. So the kinetic energy of the particle and its speed do not change: only the direction of the motion is affected. This is the single fact that decides everything else in the section, because a force of constant magnitude that is always perpendicular to the velocity is what uniform circular motion requires.
concepts.evidence: The section argues from it directly, asking whether the magnetic force causes circular motion and answering that the particle's kinetic energy and speed remain constant, and its conceptual questions ask how the motion of a charged particle distinguishes a magnetic field from an electric one.

concepts.name: A charge crossing a uniform field moves in a circle
concepts.why: When a charge moves perpendicular to a uniform field, the magnetic force is the centripetal force, so $qvB$ equals $mv^2/r$. The simplest case is worth doing carefully, because the reader has already solved circular motion in Chapter 6 and needs only to recognise which force is playing the centripetal part. In a vacuum the magnetic field is then the only thing deciding the motion, and the particle circles forever at constant speed.
concepts.evidence: Figure 22.19 draws a negative charge circling in a field into the page with the force always pointing to the centre, Figure 22.18 shows the curved bubble chamber tracks the effect produces, and the section sets $qvB = mv^2/r$ as its first equation.

concepts.name: The radius of the path, $\kr = m\kv/\kq\kBmag$
concepts.why: Solving the centripetal equation for the radius gives the mass times the speed divided by the charge times the field. Everything the rest of the chapter does with curved tracks follows from reading this fraction: a heavier particle swings wider, a faster one swings wider, and a stronger field or a larger charge pulls the circle tighter. Fixing the speed, the charge and the field makes the radius proportional to the mass, which is how a mass spectrometer weighs an ion, and it is also why an electron in a television tube is turned through a circle less than a millimetre across by a magnet held against the glass.
concepts.evidence: The result is the section's second learning objective and the only equation in its summary, Example 22.2 computes the radius for an electron in a 0.500 T field, and nine of the section's problems, among them the two mass spectrometer problems, are rearrangements of it.

concepts.name: A charge that is not perpendicular to the field spirals along it
concepts.why: Only the component of the velocity perpendicular to the field bends; the component along the field is untouched, since the magnetic force is zero for motion parallel to the lines. A particle that enters at an angle therefore circles about a field line while drifting along it, which is a spiral rather than a circle. Charged particles approaching a magnetic field are far more likely to be trapped in spiral orbits about the lines than to cross them, and that single sentence explains the aurora, the shape of the tracks in Figure 22.20 and the whole of the next idea.
concepts.evidence: The section states that the parallel component is unaffected and that this produces a spiral rather than a circular motion, Figure 22.20 shows electrons spiralling about the field lines of a magnet held to a screen, and Figure 22.22 shows cosmic rays following the Earth's field lines to the poles.

concepts.name: The magnetic mirror and the Van Allen belts
concepts.why: Where the field lines crowd together, the field grows stronger along the direction of travel, and the force then has a component that slows the particle's motion along the line and can turn it back. A region of strong field at each end therefore holds a particle bouncing between them, which is a magnetic mirror. The Earth is such a trap: particles from the Sun and from deep space are held in the two Van Allen belts, migrate along the field lines and are reflected away from the poles, and those that do enter the atmosphere near the poles light the aurora and give a higher radiation dose there than at the equator.
concepts.evidence: Figure 22.21 draws a particle turned back where the lines converge and names the effect a magnetic mirror, Figure 22.23 draws the inner and outer Van Allen belts, and the section returns to the aurora photograph that opens the chapter.

concepts.name: Magnetic fields confine and steer charged particles
concepts.why: The same trapping is built deliberately. Accelerators use magnetic fields not only to bend a beam round its ring but to focus it and hold it together against the repulsion of its own like charges. A tokamak bends a solenoid into a doughnut so that the charged particles of a plasma circle the field lines without ever reaching the wall, which is the leading hope for containing a fusion reaction. A microwave oven's magnetron holds oscillating electrons the same way. The applications are worth naming together, because they are one idea used four times.
concepts.evidence: The section gives the Fermilab accelerator in Figure 22.24 and the tokamak in Figure 22.25 as its examples, names the magnetron, and ends by pointing forward to the mass spectrometer of 22.11.

concepts.name: The Hall effect: a field pushes carriers to one side
concepts.why: A magnetic field acts on the charges moving inside a conductor just as it acts on a free charge, and since the charges cannot leave the metal, they pile up on one side and leave the other side with the opposite sign. The separated charge makes an electric field across the conductor, and that field pushes the carriers back. The pile-up therefore stops almost at once, at the point where the electric force $qE$ equals the magnetic force $qvB$, so that $E = vB$. The voltage this separation produces across the conductor is the Hall emf.
concepts.evidence: The section's first learning objective asks the reader to describe the Hall effect, Figure 22.26 draws it for negative and for positive carriers, Figure 22.27 draws the two forces in balance, and the glossary defines both the Hall effect and the Hall emf.

concepts.name: The Hall emf, $\varepsilon = Blv$
concepts.why: For a uniform field across a uniform conductor the electric field is uniform too, so the voltage is the field times the width, $E = \varepsilon/l$. Putting that into the balance gives the Hall emf as the field times the width times the speed, when the three are mutually perpendicular. It is a small voltage, tens of microvolts for blood in an artery, and the section is careful to say so, since the difficulty of measuring it against the millivolts of a heartbeat is why a Hall flow probe applies an alternating field.
concepts.evidence: The result is the section's second learning objective and the one equation in its summary, Example 22.3 computes the 80 microvolts a flow probe reads on an artery, and every problem of the section is a rearrangement of it.

concepts.name: Reading the sign of the carriers from the Hall emf
concepts.why: Reverse the sign of the carriers and, for the same conventional current, they move the other way, so the magnetic force pushes them to the same side but they carry the opposite charge there: the Hall emf changes sign. Knowing the directions of the field and the current therefore lets the reader work out the sign of whatever is carrying the current, which is how the effect was used historically to show that electrons carry the current in metals and that positive carriers do so in some semiconductors.
concepts.evidence: Figure 22.26 prints the two cases side by side with emfs of opposite sign, the section calls this one very important use of the effect, and its conceptual question asks how the effect could give the free charge density in a conductor.

concepts.name: Hall probes and flow meters
concepts.why: Two applications follow directly from the formula. Run a known current through a small conductor and the Hall emf measures the field, which is a Hall probe; they can be made very small and, once calibrated, very accurate. Or fix the field and the width and the Hall emf measures the speed of whatever is moving, which is how blood flow in an artery and water flow in a pipe are measured without touching the fluid. Here the sign of the emf depends only on the directions of the field and the velocity, not on the sign of the charges, so a fluid carrying both signs still gives a reading.
concepts.evidence: The section names the Hall probe as one of the most common uses of the effect, Figure 22.28 draws a flow probe across a tube, and five of the section's problems measure a flow or a field this way.

concepts.name: The force on a current-carrying wire, $F = IlB\sin\theta$
concepts.why: Charges cannot escape a wire, so the magnetic force on the charges moving inside it is handed on to the wire itself. Adding the force on every carrier in a length of wire, and recognising that the number of carriers per unit volume times the charge times the drift velocity times the area is the current, turns the force on one charge into a force on the wire: the current times the length in the field times the field times the sine of the angle between the current and the field. The derivation is worth following once, because it is the bridge between a law about particles and a law about circuits.
concepts.evidence: The section's second learning objective asks the reader to calculate the force, the derivation is printed in full, Example 22.4 computes the 1.50 N on 5.00 cm of wire in a strong field, and the section summary states the result.

concepts.name: The force per unit length, $F/l = IB\sin\theta$
concepts.why: Dividing by the length gives the force per metre of wire, which is the form the reader wants whenever the wire is long or its length is not given, as it is for a lightning bolt, a power line or the two parallel conductors of 22.10. It is the same result written so that only the current, the field and the angle appear.
concepts.evidence: The section divides both sides by the length and states the result, and its problems ask for the force per meter on a lightning bolt at the equator and on a hundred-metre section of a light-rail power line.

concepts.name: Right hand rule 1 with the thumb on the current
concepts.why: The direction of the force on a wire is given by the same right hand rule as the force on a single charge, with the thumb now pointing along the current rather than along one charge's velocity. The substitution is exactly right because a conventional current points the way positive carriers would move, so the rule needs no second version and the reader needs no second rule.
concepts.evidence: The first learning objective asks the reader to describe the effect of a magnetic force on a conductor, Figures 22.29 and 22.30 apply the rule to a wire between the poles of a magnet, and ten of the section's problems ask for one of the three directions given the other two.

concepts.name: Magnetohydrodynamics: pumping a fluid without moving parts
concepts.why: If the current runs through a conducting fluid rather than a wire, the force falls on the fluid and pushes it along the tube, and the pump has no moving parts at all. That is attractive for a hot or chemically active liquid such as the sodium in some nuclear reactors, for an experimental artificial heart, and for a submarine drive that would run more quietly than a propeller. The direction of the force does not depend on the sign of the carriers, so a fluid carrying both signs still moves one way.
concepts.evidence: Figure 22.31 draws the pump and Figure 22.32 the submarine duct, the section discusses why existing drives are heavy and inefficient, and two of the section's conceptual questions ask about the sign of the carriers and about why sea water works better than fresh.

concepts.name: The torque on a current loop, $\ktau = NIAB\sin\theta$
concepts.why: Put a rectangular loop of wire on a shaft in a uniform field and the forces on its two vertical sides are equal and opposite, so the loop does not move off, but each of them produces a torque about the shaft in the same sense, so the loop turns. Adding the two torques gives the width times the force, and putting $F = IlB$ into it and recognising the width times the height as the area gives the torque as the number of turns times the current times the area times the field times the sine of the angle. The derivation is done for a rectangle, and the result holds for a loop of any shape.
concepts.evidence: The section's second learning objective asks the reader to calculate the torque, the derivation runs from Figure 22.33 through the top views of Figure 22.34, Example 22.5 finds the 30.0 N·m maximum torque on a hundred-turn loop, and eight of the section's problems are rearrangements of it.

concepts.name: The torque is greatest side-on and zero face-on, and then reverses
concepts.why: The angle in the formula is between the field and the perpendicular to the loop, so the torque is greatest when the loop's plane lies along the field and falls to zero when the loop faces the field squarely. Past that point the sine changes sign and so does the torque, which means that a loop left to itself does not keep turning: it oscillates back and forth about the position of zero torque, exactly as a compass needle settles onto a field line.
concepts.evidence: The four top views of Figure 22.34 are drawn precisely to show the maximum, the zero and the reversal, the section says that unless something is done the coil will oscillate about equilibrium, and three of the section's problems ask at what angle the torque is a given fraction of its maximum.

concepts.name: A loop feels a torque but no net force
concepts.why: The forces on the top and bottom segments of the loop are vertical, parallel to the shaft, equal in size and opposite in direction, so they neither turn the loop nor push it anywhere. The forces on the two vertical sides are equal and opposite as well. The loop therefore feels no net force in a uniform field, only a torque, and a motor turns without wandering across the room.
concepts.evidence: The section notes the cancellation twice while deriving the torque and states in so many words that the net force on the loop is zero, and its conceptual question asks the reader to draw the diagram and use the right hand rule to show that the vertical forces produce no torque about the axis.

concepts.name: Brushes keep a motor turning
concepts.why: A coil that only oscillates is no use, so a motor reverses the current each time the coil passes the position of zero torque, using automatic switches called brushes. The torque then always acts the same way round and the coil keeps turning in one direction, which is how electrical energy is turned into mechanical work. This is the whole of the motor: a loop, a field, and a switch that changes the current twice a revolution.
concepts.evidence: Figure 22.35 draws the brushes at the two moments, the section explains that the angular momentum of the coil carries it through the zero and the brushes reverse the current there, and the glossary defines a motor.

concepts.name: A meter is a motor that turns only part of a turn
concepts.why: An analog meter is built the same way, but its magnet poles are shaped so that the field stays perpendicular to the loop over a wide range of angles. The sine is then always about one, the torque depends on the current and not on the angle, and a spring supplies a counter-torque that grows with the deflection, so the needle's position is proportional to the current. A sensitive galvanometer for a voltmeter or an ammeter wants a large loop area, a strong field and low-resistance coils.
concepts.evidence: Figure 22.36 draws the shaped poles, the spring and the needle, the section explains the design in full, and the glossary defines a meter.

concepts.name: The field of a long straight wire, $B = \mu_0 I/2\pi r$
concepts.why: Experiment gives the field round a long straight wire as the permeability of free space times the current, divided by two pi times the shortest distance to the wire. The field falls off as one over the distance, not one over the distance squared, and, because the wire is long, it does not depend on where along the wire the point is. The section's own example is the most useful reading of it: 25 A in a wire makes twice the Earth's field 5.0 cm away, which is why an overhead power line disturbs a surveyor's compass.
concepts.evidence: The section's first learning objective asks the reader to calculate the current that produces a magnetic field, Example 22.6 works the 25 A out, the summary states the result, and the glossary defines the magnetic field strength produced by a long straight current-carrying wire.

concepts.name: Right hand rule 2 for the field a current makes
concepts.why: Compasses set round a straight wire show that the field lines are circles centred on the wire, and the second right hand rule names the sense of the circles: point the thumb along the current and the fingers curl the way the field goes. It holds for any segment of current, not only a straight wire, which is what lets the reader read the field of a loop and of a solenoid off the same rule. The first right hand rule gives a force and this one gives a field, and keeping the two apart is most of the work.
concepts.evidence: The second learning objective asks the reader to use the rule, Figure 22.37 draws the compasses and the hand together, Figures 22.38 and 22.39 apply it to a loop and to a solenoid, and 22.11's direction problems ask for the field on each side of a current.

concepts.name: The permeability of free space
concepts.why: The constant in the field formulas, $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ T·m/A, is the permeability of free space, one of the basic constants of nature and the magnetic counterpart of the permittivity that appeared in the electric field. Its value is exact rather than measured, which is what makes the definition of the ampere in 22.10 possible, and the book notes that it is related to the speed of light, a connection the later chapters make good.
concepts.evidence: The section introduces the constant with the straight-wire field, remarks that it is one of the basic constants in nature and that it is related to the speed of light, and the glossary defines it.

concepts.name: Ampere's law and the Biot-Savart law
concepts.why: Every segment of a current makes a field like a short piece of a long straight wire, and the field of a current of any shape is the vector sum of the fields of its segments. Stating that for one segment is the Biot-Savart law, and summing it with calculus gives Ampere's law, which relates field and current in general. Ampere's law is one of Maxwell's equations, the four that describe all electromagnetic phenomena; the book keeps the general features, the right hand rule and the rules for field lines, and leaves the integrals to a later course.
concepts.evidence: The section devotes a header to Ampere's Law and Others, its glossary defines the Biot-Savart law, Ampere's law and Maxwell's equations, and the boxed note Making Connections: Relativity records that these equations led Einstein to relativity.

concepts.name: The field at the centre of a loop, $B = \mu_0 I/2R$
concepts.why: The field of a current loop is complicated everywhere except at one point, and there it is simple: at the centre it is the permeability times the current divided by twice the radius, and for a flat coil of $N$ loops it is $N$ times that. The larger the loop the weaker its centre field, because the current is further away, and the shape of the field outside the loop is the shape of a bar magnet's, which is the promise 22.2 made with its iron filings now made quantitative.
concepts.evidence: The section states the formula and its $N$-loop form, Figure 22.38 maps the field inside and outside the loop and notes that it is similar to that of a bar magnet, the glossary defines the magnetic field strength at the center of a circular loop, and three of 22.11's problems use it.

concepts.name: The field inside a solenoid, $B = \mu_0 nI$
concepts.why: Wind the wire into a long coil and the fields of the turns add inside and very nearly cancel outside, so the field inside is uniform in magnitude and direction over most of the coil's length and the field just outside is nearly zero. Its strength is the permeability times the number of turns per unit length times the current, with no radius in it at all, which is why a solenoid is how a strong and uniform field over a large volume is made, as in an MRI magnet.
concepts.evidence: The section's fourth header introduces the solenoid, Figure 22.39 draws the uniform interior and the cutaway, Example 22.7 finds 2.01 T inside a two-metre coil of 2000 turns, and the glossary defines both the solenoid and the field strength inside it.

concepts.name: The force between two parallel currents, $F/l = \mu_0 I_1 I_2/2\pi r$
concepts.why: Nothing new is needed for this result, only the two things the chapter already has: the first wire makes a field at the second, and the second wire feels a force in that field. Putting the straight-wire field into the force on a current and dividing by the length gives the force per unit length as the permeability times the two currents divided by two pi times the separation. By Newton's third law each wire feels the same size of force, which is why one number serves for both.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the result in three steps from the field of wire one, Figure 22.40 draws the wires, their fields and the forces, the summary states it, and eight of the section's problems are rearrangements of it.

concepts.name: Parallel currents attract and antiparallel currents repel
concepts.why: Following the two right hand rules round gives the sense of the force: wires carrying current the same way pull together, and wires carrying current opposite ways push apart. It is the reverse of what a reader who remembers that like charges repel will guess, and it is worth checking with the hand once, because the hot and neutral wires of an appliance cord and the two conductors of a light-rail line are everyday cases of it.
concepts.evidence: The caption of Figure 22.40 states both cases and the section repeats them in its summary, the AP item asks which way two equal parallel currents push, and the conceptual questions ask about the hot and neutral lines on a power pole and about three coplanar wires.

concepts.name: The pinch effect
concepts.why: Because parallel currents attract, a current spread over a region squeezes itself into a narrower one. In an electric arc or a plasma this is the pinch effect, and it is not a curiosity: in a large circuit breaker it concentrates the arc between the plates that are trying to interrupt the current, burning holes and sometimes igniting the equipment. The jets of ionized material in a solar flare are shaped the same way.
concepts.evidence: The section names the effect and gives all three cases, the arc, the circuit breaker and the solar plasma, immediately after stating the force law.

concepts.name: The force between wires defines the ampere
concepts.why: Putting one ampere in each of two wires one metre apart makes a force of exactly $2 \times 10^{-7}$ N/m, exactly because the permeability of free space is itself defined as exactly $4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ T·m/A. That statement, run backwards, is the operational definition of the ampere, and with it the coulomb, since one coulomb is the charge that flows in one second at one ampere. In practice a current balance uses coils a few centimetres apart rather than infinite wires, and measuring force is the most accurate way known of fixing both units.
concepts.evidence: The section works the number out and prints the official definition in a boxed note, The Ampere, and describes the current balance that realises it.

concepts.name: A mass spectrometer weighs ions by the radius of their arcs
concepts.why: The radius of a charged particle's circle is its mass times its speed divided by its charge times the field, so if the speed, the charge and the field are all fixed, the radius is simply proportional to the mass. That is a mass spectrometer: an ion source, a stage that fixes the speed, and a uniform field in which each ion swings round an arc whose width reports its mass. The charge comes in multiples of the electron's, so it is easy to allow for. The instrument identifies chemicals and biological molecules by their mass-to-charge ratios and measures the isotope tracers used in medicine.
concepts.evidence: The section opens on the radius formula and Figure 22.41 draws the whole instrument, its ion source, its velocity selector and the two arcs of two masses, and 22.5's problems separate oxygen-16 from oxygen-18 and uranium-235 from uranium-238 this way.

concepts.name: The velocity selector, $\kv = \kEf/\kBmag$
concepts.why: Cross an electric field with a magnetic field so that they push a moving charge opposite ways, and only the particles for which the two forces balance go straight through. Setting $qE$ equal to $qvB$ cancels the charge and leaves the speed as the electric field divided by the magnetic field, which means the selected speed does not depend on the charge or the mass of the particle at all and can be dialled by changing either field. It is the stage that makes a mass spectrometer's arcs mean something.
concepts.evidence: The section derives it from the balance of the two forces, the summary states that crossed fields act as a velocity filter, and two of 22.5's problems ask for the electric field and the plate voltage a selector needs.

concepts.name: Coils steer a beam of electrons
concepts.why: A cathode ray tube, an old computer monitor, an x-ray machine and a two-mile linear accelerator are all versions of the same electron gun, and many of them use magnetic fields to point the beam. Two pairs of coils, one for the vertical and one for the horizontal, bend the electrons to wherever they are wanted on the screen. The rays are called cathode rays because they start at the cathode in the gun.
concepts.evidence: The section gives the cathode ray tube its own header and Figure 22.42 draws the coils bending the beam downward with the right hand rule beside it.

concepts.name: Magnetic resonance imaging
concepts.why: Certain nuclei, hydrogen's single proton above all, have small magnetic fields of their own, like the current loops of this chapter. Put them in a strong external field and they are pushed into one of two energy states, and a radio signal of exactly the right frequency flips them between the two. The frequency that is absorbed and re-emitted depends on the nucleus, on its chemical surroundings and on the field strength, so sweeping the field across the body makes position report itself as frequency, and the strength of the returned signal reports how much of that nucleus is there. That is nuclear magnetic resonance, and imaging with it is MRI.
concepts.evidence: The section gives MRI its own header and four paragraphs, the glossary defines both magnetic resonance imaging and nuclear magnetic resonance, and the section explains the 1 to 2 T superconducting magnet, the T1 and T2 scans and functional MRI.

concepts.name: Measuring the magnetic fields of the heart and the brain
concepts.why: Currents in nerve cells and in the heart make magnetic fields like any other currents, and those fields can be recorded without touching the body: the heart's is a magnetocardiogram and the brain's a magnetoencephalogram. They are between a million and a hundred million times weaker than the Earth's field, so they are read with a SQUID, a superconducting detector that works at liquid helium temperatures. They report activity rather than structure, which is what makes them useful for epilepsy and for fetal studies and different from an electrocardiogram.
concepts.evidence: The section gives the two recordings their own header and defines both in the glossary, describes the SQUID, and closes by noting that clinical studies have not verified the claims made for magnetic cures.
